newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ share market closes at 2-1/2 year high.
newsitem.headline: NZ share market closes at 2-1/2 year high.

text.p: New Zealand's share market decisively shrugged off concerns over Saturday's general election when it powered 1.36 percent ahead to close at a 2-1/2 year high on Monday.
Two weekend polls showed a strong swing to the centre-left at the expense of the conservative ruling National Party, but the Dow's 60 point rise on Friday was the greater influence, brokers said.
"What polls, what election?" quipped First NZ Capital broker David Price. "It's absolutely amazing." The NZSE-40 index rose 30.48 points to 2,274.76, its highest since March 1994.
"It was a phenomenal day. It was partly the Dow and partly interest rates," said Hendry Hay McIntosh broker Tim Koller.
Investors were surprised at the strength of the market just days before the election, and revised plans to sell, he said.
Volume was a healthy $88.7 million with over a third of that being in the day's star performer, market heavyweight Telecom.
It ended up 15 cents at an all-time high of $7.20.

Most other leaders were strong with the exception of Carter Holt Harvey, which was down one to $3.24. The Fletcher family of stocks were strong, with Fletcher Building up 12 cents to $3.62 and Fletcher Energy up 10 at $3.60.
Koller said five successive up-days showed the market was gathering momentum and he saw the possibility of further gains.

Two polls at the weekend showed a steep rise in support for the centre-left Labour Party mainly at the expense of the conservative ruling National Party. The polls suggested the three parties of the left would be well positioned to form a government after the october 12 election.

Ord Minnett Equities Director John Rattray said the market had never priced in re-election of the centre-right and was comfortable with the centre-left Labour Party, whose economic policies are seen differing little from National.
The weekend polls may have even clarified the situation for markets -- showing Labour would definitely be the senior partner in any alliance with the nationalist New Zealand First Party.
"There's definitely some reassurance for the market because (Labour finance spokesman) Michael Cullen as finance minister is regarded as relatively dry," Rattray said.
Wilson & Horton gained 17 cents to $10.74 after independent directors said they were negotiating with Ireland's Independent Newspapers Plc to increase its bid for the newspaper publisher.
